To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) identifiability of victims is associated with more mental imagery, which in turn is associated with higher levels of victim-focused feelings, and that (b) victim numbers are associated with higher levels and more negative donor-focused feelings.

(a) identified victims elicit more vivid imagery than non-identified victims; (b) vivid imagery is related to more positive affect and higher donations; (c) the number of victims affects the vividness of imagery and donations; and (d) the number of victim effect operates through the impact of the event.
(1) identifiability and (2) number of victims have (3) different psychological effects, which are mediated by (4) different affective and cognitive processes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how different types of information about victims affect the cognitive processes of perceived impact and affective responses of donors, and thus ultimately their charitable donations.
the psychological processes that underlie the effects of identifiability and number of victims on charitable donations.
the psychological processes that are related to the effects of identifiability and number of victims and their impact on donation decisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
identifiability increases donations because people feel more compassion and empathy for identifiable victims, which in turn increases their impact judgments and mental images.
identifiability effects operate through mental imagery, impact, and donor-focused feelings, whereas victim number effects operate only through mental imagery and impact.
the effects of identifiability and of victim number on charitable donations are mediated by different psychological processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the identified victim effect is mediated by the cognitive mechanism of mental imagery and that the victim number effect is mediated by impact judgments and donor-focused feelings.
the identifiability effect is mediated by impact judgments and mental image vividness and that the victim number effect is mediated by the affective motivation to help victims.
the identifiability effect is mainly driven by mental imagery and impact judgments, whereas the victim number effect is driven by donor-focused feelings and the impact judgments.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of identifiability and number on donations are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but can co-occur and are driven by different psychological mechanisms.
the identified victim effect is not just a matter of empathy or sympathy, as is commonly assumed.
the effects of victim identifiability and number are not only related to the amount of money people donate, but also to the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive their decisions.
